questions.title: Audit Logging with @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate
questions.question: How do you implement automatic audit logging (created/modified timestamps and users) in Spring Data JPA?
questions.direct_answer: Enable Spring Data JPA auditing with @EnableJpaAuditing, extend an @MappedSuperclass with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, and @LastModifiedBy fields. Implement AuditorAware<T> to supply the current user. Spring Data automatically populates these fields on persist and update.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Data JPA feature knowledge and ability to avoid boilerplate by using framework capabilities.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PrePersist/@PreUpdate lifecycle callbacks manually instead of Spring Data auditing, leading to duplicated code across entities.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss using Instant vs LocalDateTime for timestamps, how @EnableJpaAuditing interacts with the ApplicationContext, and plugging in the current user from Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder inside AuditorAware.

sections.title: Manual @PrePersist Timestamps Are the Problem Spring Data Auditing Already Solved
sections.content:
Most developers implement audit logging by adding `@PrePersist` and `@PreUpdate` callbacks with `LocalDateTime.now()` in every entity. This works but leads to **duplicated code across entities**, inconsistent timestamp handling, and no clean way to capture the current user without injecting `SecurityContextHolder` into entity classes.

Spring Data's `@EnableJpaAuditing` solves all three problems with a single mechanism. Annotate fields with `@CreatedDate`, `@LastModifiedDate`, `@CreatedBy`, and `@LastModifiedBy`. Spring Data hooks into the persistence lifecycle and populates these fields automatically — timestamps from the clock, users from an `AuditorAware<T>` bean that reads `SecurityContextHolder`.

The setup uses a `@MappedSuperclass` base entity with the audit fields, so every entity inherits auditing without repeating annotations. The `@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)` annotation wires the listener that intercepts persist and update events. **Without `@EnableJpaAuditing` on a configuration class, these annotations are silently ignored** — timestamps stay null, no error is thrown, and the bug is invisible until someone checks the database. This silent failure is the single most common setup mistake.

sections.title: Setting Up Auditing — Base Entity, AuditorAware, and Timestamp Type Choice
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@EnableJpaAuditing` on a `@Configuration` class activates the auditing infrastructure** — without it, `@CreatedDate`, `@LastModifiedDate`, `@CreatedBy`, `@LastModifiedBy` annotations are silently ignored.
- **`AuditorAware<T>` provides the current user for `@CreatedBy` and `@LastModifiedBy`** — implement it to return the current principal from `SecurityContextHolder`; Spring calls it on every persist/update.
- **`Instant` over `LocalDateTime` for audit timestamps** — `Instant` is always UTC; `LocalDateTime` carries no timezone and behaves differently across JVM timezone settings.
- **`@MappedSuperclass AuditableEntity` shares audit fields across all entities** — define `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `createdBy`, `modifiedBy` once; every entity extends it.
- **Bulk `@Modifying` queries bypass Spring Data Auditing** — update `lastModifiedAt = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` in the JPQL expression explicitly; the auditing infrastructure only hooks into entity state changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA Auditing automates the bookkeeping that every entity needs: who created this, when, who last changed it. Setting it up correctly once in a `@MappedSuperclass` covers every entity in the application.

**Setup**
- Add `@EnableJpaAuditing` to a `@Configuration` class (or `@SpringBootApplication`)
- Create a `@MappedSuperclass` with the audit fields:
  - `@CreatedDate Instant createdAt`
  - `@LastModifiedDate Instant updatedAt`
  - `@CreatedBy String createdBy`
  - `@LastModifiedBy String modifiedBy`
- Extend this superclass in every entity

**Providing the current user**
- Implement `AuditorAware<String>` as a `@Bean`
- Return `Optional.of(SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName())`
- Spring calls this on every INSERT and UPDATE to populate `@CreatedBy` / `@LastModifiedBy`

**`Instant` vs `LocalDateTime`**
- `Instant` is always UTC — safe across timezones and server relocations
- `LocalDateTime` is timezone-naive — different JVM timezones produce inconsistent values

Add `@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)` to the superclass — this is the hook that Spring Data uses to intercept entity lifecycle events and populate audit fields.

questions.question: How does HikariCP connection pooling work in Spring Boot, and how do you configure and tune it?
questions.title: HikariCP Connection Pool — Configuration and Tuning in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: HikariCP is Spring Boot's default connection pool. It maintains a pool of reusable database connections, avoiding the overhead of creating new connections per request. Key settings are maximumPoolSize (default 10), minimumIdle (defaults to maximumPoolSize), and connectionTimeout (30 seconds). Undersizing causes request queuing; oversizing wastes database resources and can reduce throughput due to context switching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands connection pool sizing and its impact on application performance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting maximumPoolSize to 100 thinking more connections means better performance — database servers perform worse with many concurrent connections due to CPU context switching and lock contention.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the formula connections = (2 * CPU cores) + disk spindles, explain leak detection with leakDetectionThreshold, and discuss how @Transactional scope affects connection hold time.

sections.title: 100 Connections Doesn't Mean 100x Throughput — It Usually Means Worse Performance
sections.content:
Developers set `maximumPoolSize=100` thinking more connections means more throughput. **The opposite is often true.** A PostgreSQL benchmark by the HikariCP team showed that **a pool of 10 connections outperformed a pool of 100** on the same hardware. More connections means more CPU context switching, more lock contention in the database, and more memory consumed per connection.

The general formula is **connections = (2 × CPU cores) + effective disk spindles.** For an 8-core database server with SSDs, that's roughly 17-20 connections. Going beyond this doesn't increase parallelism — it increases contention.

HikariCP is Spring Boot's default connection pool. It starts with `minimumIdle` connections (defaults to `maximumPoolSize`) and grows up to `maximumPoolSize` (default 10). When a request needs a connection and none are available, it waits up to `connectionTimeout` (30 seconds) before throwing an exception. **Undersized pools cause request queuing; oversized pools waste database resources and reduce throughput.** The pool size is the single most impactful configuration setting for database performance in a Spring Boot application.

sections.title: Critical Configuration Properties and Leak Detection
sections.content:
The most important properties for production tuning affect how long connections are held and how failures are detected.

**`maximumPoolSize`** should match your database's capacity divided by the number of application instances. 4 instances sharing a database with 80 max connections = 20 per instance, minus overhead for admin/migration connections.

**`connectionTimeout`** (default 30s) is how long a thread waits for a connection. In high-traffic APIs, 30 seconds is too long — the request is already timed out at the load balancer. Set it to 2-5 seconds and fail fast.

**`leakDetectionThreshold`** logs a warning when a connection is held longer than the threshold without being returned. Set it to the expected maximum query time (e.g., 10 seconds). **Connection leaks** — code that acquires a connection but doesn't close it — are the most common pool exhaustion cause. HikariCP logs the stack trace of the leak point, making it straightforward to find.

**`@Transactional` scope directly affects connection hold time.** A transaction holds a connection for its entire duration. A `@Transactional` method that calls an external HTTP service holds a database connection while waiting for the response — wasting pool capacity on network I/O.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Optimal pool size ≠ largest pool size** — the HikariCP formula: `connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count`; for a 4-core server without spinning disk: 9 connections; more connections increase context switching overhead.
- **`connectionTimeout` vs `maxLifetime` vs `idleTimeout`** — `connectionTimeout`: how long to wait for a pool connection (default 30s); `maxLifetime`: maximum age of a connection before recycling (default 30 min); `idleTimeout`: how long idle connections survive.
- **`leakDetectionThreshold` identifies connection leaks** — set to 2000ms in development; if a connection is held for longer, HikariCP logs the stack trace showing where it was borrowed.
- **`maximumPoolSize` also caps JDBC concurrency** — if all pool connections are in use, threads block waiting for one; pool exhaustion under load means requests queue, latency spikes, and timeouts cascade.
- **`spring.datasource.hikari.*` properties map directly to HikariCP config** — `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10`, `spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=20000`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HikariCP is Spring Boot's default connection pool — chosen for its low overhead and consistent throughput. Misconfiguring the pool size is one of the most common sources of database-related performance problems.

**Pool size — the counter-intuitive formula**
- More connections ≠ better performance
- Each database connection requires a thread on the database server; too many connections increase CPU context switching
- HikariCP's recommended formula: `(2 × CPU cores) + effective spindle count`
- For a 4-core server with SSD storage: 9 connections; most teams set 20-50 without understanding the tradeoff

**Key timeouts**
- `connectionTimeout` (30s default) — how long a thread waits for an available connection from the pool; if exceeded, throws `SQLTimeoutException`
- `maxLifetime` (30 min default) — maximum age of a connection before HikariCP closes it and opens a new one; prevents stale connections to databases that have a connection idle timeout
- `idleTimeout` (10 min default) — how long idle connections sit before being closed, down to `minimumIdle`

**Diagnosing problems**
- `leakDetectionThreshold=2000` — logs a stack trace if a connection is held for more than 2 seconds; identifies missing `close()` or unbounded transactions
- Expose HikariCP metrics via Actuator/Micrometer: `hikaricp.connections.active`, `hikaricp.connections.pending` — alert when pending connections spike
